I suppose that something like a Kalman filter could be used to update the log posterior by marginalizing over the latents rather than explicitly calculating them. But I'd need to think about it more.

On Fri, Nov 30, 2012 at 6:38 PM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:

> On Friday, November 30, 2012 5:02:00 PM UTC-5, Jeffrey Arnold wrote:

> >
> > I've been doing a lot of dynamic linear model-type models in Stan. I was wondering if for DLMs, would it (a) make sense and (b) be feasible to have a Kalman filter function in Stan?
> > For a set of latent state parameters, would it be more efficient to calculate the log posterior contribution using Kalman filter "distribution"?
>
> Do you have a specific link for your proposal? The first thing that comes to my mind are that the multivariate normal distribution is very slow in Stan, so it might be faster in theory but slower in practice (due to Stan's need to auto-diff it). Also, Stan would need something that pertains to a joint distribution rather than a conditional distribution of the latents given the observed variables.
>

The hardware has less to do with the wall time than the software, and you've coded it in the slowest possible way for a model like this. The only real benefit for a CPU like that is that you can do 8 chains at once.

> However, after 43 hours, it is about 50% complete.  Curious to see what some of the samples looked like, I had a look at the samples.csv output file.  Much to my surprise, all of the samples appear to have the exact same values.  All of them - the same.

The only thing that I can see that is really wrong with your code is that real eta[N] should be declared at the start of the model {} block, rather than inside that loop, i.e.

model {
  real eta[N];
  ...

but I don't think that would cause all the proposals to get rejected. I suspect that the default starting values are inappropriate for your data, but even then I wouldn't expect every proposal to be rejected.

So, I would try taking out the group and program effects. If that model runs, add the group effects back. If that model runs, add the program effects back. Etc. That will help you narrow down the problem.

Ben

On Sunday, December 2, 2012 2:35:41 PM UTC-5, Noah wrote:
> I still have  a lot to learn about hierarchical models.
>
> Will try your suggestions and report back to the group what I find.

It's not so much about hierarchical models in the statistical sense; it is more about understanding the differences between a Gibbs sampler like BUGS and a Hamiltonian Monte Carlo sampler, particularly one like Stan that utilizes auto-differentiation. There's not a whole lot that can be done to accelerate a BUGS model because it just figures out the corresponding DAG and sequentially samples from each conditional distribution. With Stan, various parameterizations that are statistically equivalent can perform very differently in practice and can take different amounts of time to do so, largely depending on how much burden they put on the auto-differentiation mechanism.

Ben

This is all given a particular distribution over parameters
that is being modeled.

The one thing that we can do in Stan that is like what you
can do in BUGS/JAGS is reparameterize.  It has a slightly
different effect and motivation for HMC, where
it's largely about making the posterior geometry more friendly,
which is usually an issue of making it more homogeneous in
curvature throughout the posterior probability mass that should
be sampled.

- Bob

You should also try running with the test_grad option (available
in R and command line versions), which will at least show you
what the initial parameters and gradients look like.  If any of
those are NaN or infinite (or close to infinite), it will highlight
where the problem in the model specification is.  This should run
quickly unless there are a whole lot of parameters.  (The next
version of Stan we release will run the finite differences involved
in test_grad much faster;  we should probably also have an option
to turn finite diffs off, which will still allow users to debug
with the analytic auto-diff results from Stan without the time
consumption of finite diffs.)

- Bob

> Ben,
>
> 1) I'll try an intercept now and report back.

In addition, it would be good to start the chain with an intercept equal to the log of the mean value of count. Everything else can start at zero or zero on average.

> 2) What values am i looking for and where in the gradient output?    (I need to learn how to interpret this properly to diagnose things myself.)

What you want to see is a log-posterior value that is something sane (not on the order of -1e70) and that the auto-differentiated gradient is equal to the numerically-differentiated gradient. But numeric derivatives are not going to be accurate when the starting values put you at a virtually flat spot in the log-posterior.

Ben

>
> But I think a better route would be to optimize the .stan file and hopefully circumvent this bug. For a fixed correlation matrix, multi_normal is unnecessarily slow.

Hi Ben,

I realised multi_normal would be slow, but I thought I'd use it to get the code working, and then optimise later. Thanks for the advice on how to do that! I fixed the typos in the code you sent me below, and in Stan 1.0.3, it still parses but doesn't compile (same error). And the .cpp file you sent me would also not compile with my g++. Also, I take your point about using a link function. I was going to use a logit, but since it isn't vectorised, I couldn't figure out how to index the rows of mmat. I RTFM and realised to get row i, use mmat[i] NOT mmat[i,] , as I was used to from R. I incorporated the logit link but still the same problem. I'm looking forward to Stan version 1.0.4!

Thanks again,

Simon.

> You could do
>

> data {
>     int<lower=1> N; // Number of rows
>     int<lower=1> K; // Number of beta parameters
>     matrix[N, K] mmat; // model matrix
>     vector[N] decline; // dependent variable
>     corr_matrix[N] Sigma; // phylogenetic correlation matrix
> }
>
> transformed data {
>     matrix[N,N] L;
>     Lt <- transpose(cholesky_decompose(inverse(Sigma)));
> }
>
> parameters {
>     vector[K] beta; // regression parameters
>     real<lower=0> g; // dispersion parameter
>     vector[N] species; // random effect for species
> }
>
> transformed parameters {
>     vector[N] a; // parameter for beta distn
>     vector[N] b; // parameter for beta distn

>
>     vector<lower=0,upper=1>[N] mvals; // mean values for s!
>  pecies

>
>     mvals <- mmat*beta + species;
>     a <- mvals*g; // reparameterise for beta dist
>     b  <- (1.0-mvals)*g; // reparameterise
> }
>
> model {
> //priors
>     beta ~ normal(0, 1000);
>     g ~ gamma(0.001, 0.001); // dispersion parameter
>     lp <- lp - 0.5 * dot_self(Lt * species); // MVN
>
> //likelihood
>
>     decline ~ beta(a, b);
> }

>
> where -0.5 * dot_self(Lt * species) is proportional to a multivariate normal density with correlation matrix Sigma. Also, I put the required bounds on mvals, which will cause the proposal to be rejected if any are outside the unit interval and thus may not be efficient. You could also use a loop with a logistic or normal link function here. Although these are not vectorized, loops are pretty cheap unless they are updating the log-posterior.
>
> Ben

messages.subject_clean: Help vectorising a hierarchical binomial regression
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

First of all, thanks for the great effort at bringing this stuff to the community! Stan is (going to be) great. I had previously played around with JAGS models but found that they were taking ages to converge and producing highly autocorrelated output; Stan by comparison does marvelously.

I am new to Stan, so apologies if this question is redundant. I couldn't find a similar question/answer on the forums. I am mostly fitting hierarchical GLMs to binary data, with two additional parameters to scale the expected values of the sigmoids (upper and lower bounds). This is working great, but in an effort to speed up my code I would like to vectorize where possible. Unfortunately I'm getting quite confused by the documentation so I came here for help.

Short question: can the model given on page 50 of the manual for Hierarchical Logistic Regression (section 10.7, version 1.0.3) be vectorized such that the loop over individual observations (n in 1:N) can be removed?

As I understand it, this would require the creation of a vector of integers (e.g. something like vector[N] int y), which as far as I can see in the documentation is currently not possible (only an array of integers of length N).

My model is approximately the same with a few extra parameters. I can attach a script later if you think it is helpful, but solving this for the model given in section 10.7 would do the trick.

Thanks

Tom Wallis

messages.body_plain:
Sorry about this -- we're working hard to get the
next Stan release ready.  Version 1.0.3 broke the
location reporting for error messages.

The first problem with the model is that
"class" is a reserved word.  So I changed "class" to "clazz"
(it's the usual replacement because "class" is reserved
in C++ and in Java), which highlighted the real error:

INVALID COMMAND-LINE ARGUMENT
EXPECTATION FAILURE LOCATION: file=../temp2/noah.stan; line=41, column=87

         mu[i] <- 1 + clazz_effect[clazz[N]] + b_var_1 * var_1[i]  + b_var_2 * var_2[i];
                                                                                       ^-- here

DIAGNOSTIC(S) FROM PARSER:

no matches for function name="multiply"
     arg 0 type=real[1]
     arg 1 type=real
no matches for function name="add"

     arg 0 type=real

     arg 1 type=ill formed
no matches for function name="multiply"
     arg 0 type=real[1]
     arg 1 type=real
no matches for function name="add"
     arg 0 type=ill formed
     arg 1 type=ill formed
expression is ill formed
Parser expecting: <eps>

The problem is that we don't have scalar-array mulitplication.
So trying to mulitply an array (b_var_2) by a scalar
(var_2[i]) is undefined.

If you change the array types to vector types, the arithmetic
should work as you expect.  For instance, change the declaration

     real b_var_2[N];

to

     vector[N] b_var_2;

The I/O is the same for both, so you shouldn't see any difference
in the model itself.

- Bob

This is the clue: multiplication is not defined for two things you want to multiply. In particular,

>         mu[i] <- 1 + class_effect[class[N]] + b_var_1 * var_1[i]  + b_var_2 * var_2[i];

b_var_1 and b_var_2 are of length N. You presumably intended for b_var_1 and b_var_2 to be scalars or maybe meant to write b_var_1[i] * var_1[i] + b_var_2[i] * var_2[i]. Also, class[N] should presumably be class[i]. Also, as of Stan v1.0.4, you won't be able to declare and use a variable called class because that is a reserved word in C++, but you could declare and use a variable called Class. Also, doing a model like this the BUGS way will be slow and inefficient in Stan.

Ben

On 12/10/12 2:50 PM, Noah Silverman wrote:

 > Didn't know about the reserved variable.  Good catch!

The reserved word list is in the 1.0.3 doc, but the
parser wasn't trapping uses.  In 1.0.4, the stanc parser
will catch the reserved words and report them as errors.
(Otherwise you'd just get errors when trying to compile the
C++ generated by Stan, which we want to eliminate so that
Stan users never ever have to think about C++.)

> 1) I thought that the betas of a model are scaler, and that we just sample them repeatedly from the posterior. (At least
> that's how it appears with bugs/jags.)

I'm not sure what you mean by "betas of a model" -- you don't
have variables named "beta", so I assume you mean what
you declared as arrays, b_var_1 and b_var_2.

The problem is that Stan doesn't support

    real x[N];
    real y[N];
    real c;

    y <- x * c; // ILL FORMED

It does support:

    vector[N] x;
    vector[N] y;
    real c;

    y <- x * c; // OK

> 2) You mentioned that my structure will be "slow and inefficient" in stan.  Is there a faster/better way?

See my follow up message.  Ben may have other ideas.

- Bob

On Tuesday, December 11, 2012 5:16:32 PM UTC-5, Tom Wallis wrote:
> In that file there's a typo in which sigma[g,d] was commented out. Fixed in this attachment.

You don't need to explicitly specify uniform priors. But, if you intend to use a uniform(0,100) prior, you should restrict the upper bound of sigma as well, with:

vector<lower=0,upper=100>[D] sigma[G];

Another potential problem is p failing to be in the (0,1) interval. You might try declaring p at the top of the model {} block and doing something like

  for (n in 1:N) {
    p <- gamma + (1 - gamma) * Phi(x[n] * beta[ss[n]]);
    p <- if_else(step(1.0 - p), p, 0.99999);
    y[n] ~ bernoulli(p); # fitting as a cumulative normal (probit) model.
  }

Although if that step() ever binds after the warmup phase, then there are modeling issues.

Ben

> One issue is that you have:
>
>    sigma[g,d] ~ uniform(0,100);
>
> but declare sigma as:
>
>    vector<lower=0>[D] sigma[G]; # population level standard deviation on the beta weights.
>
> What you want is to declare sigma with a constraint
> that matches the support of its sampling distribution, i.e.,
>
>     vector<lower=0,upper=100>[D] sigma[G];
>
> With the constraint in place, the sampling statement
> isn't even needed, as the constraint places a uniform
> distribution on sigma over its support [0,100].  You can
> include it for clarity -- the Stan compiler is smart enough to
> simply eliminate the unnecessary computation (we can
> figure out which parts of a probability function are needed up
> to a constant based on the parameter vs. data declarations).
>
> It turns out that I ran the .Rdata file without
> knowing it after I downloaded everything.  So much for

> You can make things much faster by vectorizing, as in

> with

messages.body_plain:
Sorry -- wasn't looking closely enough at your input.
Like the dump() function in R, stan_rdump() wants
just the names of the variables to dump in the list.
You can supply an optional environment from which to
read the variables.  (I'm barely an R novice myself,
so I feel your pain with R's odd conventions, which we
followed in the design of RStan.)

- Bob

> Thanks Bob.
>
> On Point 3, when I simply passed the list stanDat (defined above) to stan_rdump as
>

>
>

>      > Dear Bob and Ben,

>      > Thanks for the suggestions. Sorry about the binary file Bob.

>
>     I don't know what the problem is on your side.  Did

>     fine.
>
>     We need to put something in that'll allow variable inits,
>     but less diffuse than (-2,2) uniform on the unconstrained
>     scale.  (That'll init positive scale parameters in the range

>     from where an actual sample from the posterior would

>      >      arg 1 type=real
>      >      arg 2 type=real
>      > expression is ill formed

>      >
>      > p was declared as real at the top of the model block so not sure what's going on there.
>
>     The first argument needs to be an int.  That's
>     why Ben was using step().  We're adding general
>     comparison and boolean operators in the next release,
>     so this should be easier.
>
>

>

>      > |

>     then sure
>
>
>      > 4. Thanks for the vectorising tips. I was aware that my code could be vectorised but I attempted to do so today
>     and got
>      > errors with the multiplication for x[n] * beta[ss[n]] within the cumulative normal statement (could not find
>     function
>      > "multiply", meaning I suppose that the beta (changed to type matrix) and the row vector x[n] were not conformable).
>
>     if x[n] is a ROW vector and beta[ss[n]] is a matrix, then you should
>     be able to do x[n] * beta[ss[n]].  The error message will tell you
>     what types it thought you were giving it.   Here, beta is

messages.body_plain:
Ok, so I got stan_rdump working by making sure all the variables I would pass in the list to the stan function of rstan are in the workspace, then using the command:

stan_rdump(list('N', 'y', 'D', 'x', 'ss', 'S', 'gg', 'G', 'gamma'),file='myDump.Rdump')

Incidentally, since rstan users are often passing data to stan as a list in R, I think an example of how to get that list of data to be output by stan_rdump would be great to have in the stan_rdump documentation.

I've attached my model (.txt file) and my data (myDump.txt) here.

I run stan through rstan using the following command:

initial.fit <- stan(model_code = stanModel1, data = stanDat, iter = 1, chains = 4, seed = 1, test_grad=TRUE, init=0)

Note that inits are set to zero and the seed is set to 1.

For this data and this model on my computer (and also on my home computer), I get the same sampling error: 'error occurred during calling the sampler; sampling not done'. I've pasted the full output below.

Any ideas why this fails on my machines but not for you?

Thanks

Tom

Maybe a made an error in translating my code from JAGS to STAN?

The population of ducks at time 1 is a parameter for population at time 2.

delta_log_ducks[t-1,z] <- Sg[z] - dd[z]*log(true_ducks[t-1,z]);

true_ducks[t,z] <- exp(log(true_ducks[t-1,z]) + delta_log_ducks[t-1,z]+ Zeta[t-1,z] + shock_ducks[t-1,z]);

I could in theory I guess I could fit the exact same model at year 1 that I fit for all  the other years but then my population at year 1 would be dependent on year 0 for which I have no information. Instead I would rather use the information I have at year 1 (i.e the population estimates and s.e.) to start the model.

In his current form the model has to start at a definitive value (i.e the population estimate at year 1) which bugs me a bit. I would rather acknowledge the uncertainty in the populations estimate and draw the population at year 1 from a normal distribution with the s.e that has been estimated from the survey.

My apologies if I sound a little dense.

Chris

messages.body_plain:
Hi there,

I am fitting hierarchical glms to binomial data. I tried vectorising one of my models to speed it up. The model compiles and runs just fine, but my "vectorised" version ("model2.txt") runs much slower than the original ("model1.txt"). It took 18 seconds for 100 samples of 4 chains for model 1, and 96 seconds for model 2. I've also attached some test data that will allow you to run the models.

Always clear everything between speed tests.  In fact,
I'd suggest restarting R from scratch.

Stan uses R's environment for memory, so you just need
to get rid of the fit object and anything you've attached.

I can't imagine a situation in which the vectorized
versions will be slower -- the vectorized code should
be both faster and consume less memory.  As Ben said in a
previous note, you probably don't want to use col() for
optimal performance, but it should still be faster than
not vectorizing.

- Bob

> I'm not sure if this is the desired behaviour for that argument (I thought it printed all evaluations?).

It doesn't sample when test_grad is used.  We should
remove the error message, because it's not an error,
but rather not trying to sample on purpose.

> In any case, it is the inits that were causing the original error I posted as you suspected. If inits are set to zero
> the model gets through the samples just fine (though I assume in this case I can't really use the Rhat values, since the
> initial values were not diffuse);

You can still use the Rhat values.  There's still randomness.
In fact, the very first step will choose momenta that will take
you away from 0 pretty quickly.  That's why you'll see lots of
movement in the traceplots and you'll see Rhat values well above
1.

You always have a problem with Rhat that it's only a rejection
test.  If Rhat values are not near 1, you know you haven't converged.
But if they're near 1, you don't know that you have converged.

> if inits are set to random then the sampler fails with the error "Initialization
> failed after 100 attempts.  Try specifying initial values, reducing ranges of constrained values, or reparameterizing
> the model."
>
> Thanks for all your help sorting this out. Any recommendations for how to proceed with these models? Set my own inits?

You can set your own inits based on previous output and then
add some noise.  But you'll have to put them back onto the constrained
scale of the model.  The auto-init is on the unconstrained (transformed
param) scale.

We're going to add a feature that will add a little noise around
user-specified inits for just this situation.

The root of the problem is that there's only so much arithmetic
precision out there from which to recover.  In theory, we'd be fine
if we had arbitrary precision arithmetic (though it might be slow
to converge).  But regression problems are really taxing because of
the form of the likelihood, so there's only so much overdispersion in the
inits that remains arithmetically tractable.

- Bob

On 12/12/12 4:09 PM, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> Should we perhaps suggest that examples be sent with preset seeds, to aid replicability?  I would prefer fixed seeds than inits=0 as a default!

Even without preset seeds, Stan dumps out the seed as part
of the output to allow replication.

The problem arises when the sampler can't recover from
parameter settings that are too far away from where they
should be.

I'm having this same problem with the model I'm working
on for data annotation, so I take some crude empirical
estimates of some parameters as a starting point.

By fitting with inits=0, you get a feeling for where the
solution is, which will then let you do some inits with
noise around that.

We might also consider lowering the initial dispersion
from [-2,2] to something more modest.  That's a pretty
big range for a regression problem with lots of coeffs.

- Bob

On Thursday, December 13, 2012 4:28:56 PM UTC-5, Tom Wallis wrote:
> Just spotted one problem in Model 3. In the model block I'm giving beta a prior based on mu and sigma, whereas I think this line should be deleted and the prior is the unit normal on e_beta; beta will get contributions from mu and sigma by the transformed parameter block.
>
> This can't explain the speed issues though.

Yes, that was a problem. When using the Matt trick, always put the prior on the thing in the parameters {} block, which implies a prior on the thing in the transformed parameters {} block, but if you explicitly put a prior on the thing in the transformed parameters {} block, you will get the wrong posterior.

I have made some changes so that model1 is equivalent to model2 and the latter is slightly faster. The gain in speed should depend mostly on D, which is only 4 in this case. Originally, in model1 x was declared as

row_vector[D] x[N]; # vector of predictor values for each trial.

and accessed by

p <- gamma + (1 - gamma - lambda[ss[n]]) * Phi(x[n] * beta[ss[n]]);

whereas in model 2 (and 3) x was declared as

matrix[N,D] x; # design matrix for linear model.

and accessed by

p <- gamma + (1 - gamma - lambda[ss[n]]) * Phi(dot_product(row(x,n),row(beta,ss[n])));

Apparently the first way is faster, but I have harmonized on the second way until we sort about the bigger issue: model3 is still not equivalent to the other two for some reason that I haven't been able to spot in the .stan code or in the C++ code.

Ben

On 12/13/12 6:10 PM, Ben Goodrich wrote:

> I have made some changes so that model1 is equivalent to model2 and the latter is slightly faster. The gain in speed
> should depend mostly on D, which is only 4 in this case. Originally, in model1 x was declared as
>
> |
>
> row_vector[D] x[N]; # vector of predictor values for each trial.
>
> and accessed by
>

> ... x[n] ...

>

> whereas in model 2 (and 3) x was declared as
>
> matrix[N,D] x; # design matrix for linear model.
>
> and accessed by
>

> ... row(x,n) ...

>
> Apparently the first way is faster,

Yes.  The reason is that for arrays, Stan uses
nested std::vector objects in C++.  That means
pulling out a "row" of a vector<vector<double> >
can return a reference to an existing object
rather than allocating and copying.

Although I'm the only one who finds it natural,
x[n] returns the same result as row(x,n).

Now if we didn't mangle Eigen's expression templates,
we could deal with row() and column() without copying,
too, and column() would be efficient because the data's
local due to the column-major order we use for Eigen
matrices.

- Bob

> commenting out the uniform prior on sigma).

The whole point of reparameterizing is to change the geometry of the
posterior in the parameters in the "parameters" block.   The goal
of the transforms is to make the posterior geometry closer to
Euclidean and hence easier to traverse stably with HMC.  In particular,
we want to try to remove position (i.e., parameter) dependent curvature
and scaling as much as possible.

Michael B and I are about to add auto-diff for Hessians and Hessian-vector
products, so we'll soon be able to inspect the curvature implications of
the transformations.

messages.body_plain:
You mean the inverse-scale parameter set close to 0, right? And don't
you also need to set the shape parameter very close to 0?

To my mind it's simpler and clearer to just code it up directly using lp__:

lp__ <- lp__ - log(a);

Note that this is an improper prior, since the integral of 1/a from 0
to infinity diverges. It's equivalent to a uniform distribution on log
a, so if you wanted to get fancy you could also write

parameters {
  real loga;
}
transformed parameters {
  real<lower=0> a;
  a <- exp(loga);
}
model {
  # p(loga) \propto 1
}

Matt

for more accurate simulations and therefore smaller step sizes. Should
be easier (and better calibrated) than trying to set epsilon by hand.

messages.subject: Stan 1.1.0 and RStan 1.1.0
messages.subject_clean: Stan 1.1.0 and RStan 1.1.0
messages.body_plain:
We're happy to announce the availability of Stan and RStan
versions 1.1.0.  Information on downloading and installing and
using them is available as always from the Stan home page:

    http://mc-stan.org/

v1.1.0 Release Notes
======================================================================
-- Backward Compatibility Issue
    * Categorical distribution recoded to match documentation;  it
      now has support {1,...,K} rather than {0,...,K-1}.
    * (RStan) change default value of permuted flag from FALSE to TRUE for
      Stan fit S4 extract() method
-- New Features
    * Conditional (if-then-else) statements
    * While statements
-- New Functions
    * generalized multiply_lower_tri_self_transpose() to non-square
      matrices
    * special functions: log_inv_logit(), log1m_inv_logit()
    * matrix special functions: cumulative_sum()
    * probability functions: poisson_log_log() for log-rate
      parameterized Poisson
    * matrix functions: block(), diag_pre_multiply(), diag_post_multiply()
    * comparison operators (<, >, <=, >=, ==, !=)
    * boolean operators (!, ||, &&)
    * allow +/- inf values in variable declaration constraints
-- RStan Improvements
    * get_posterior_mean() method for Stan fit objects
    * replaced RcppEigen dependency with include of Eigen source
    * added read_stan_csv() to create Stan fit object from CSV files of
      the form written to disk by the command-line version of Stan
    * as.data.frame() S3 method for Stan fit objects
-- Bug Fixes
    * fixed bug in NUTS diagonal resulting in too small step sizes
    * fixed bug introduced in 1.0.3 that hid line and column number
      bug reporting
    * added checks that data dimensions match as well as sizes
    * removed non-symmetric versions of eigenvalues() and eigenvectors()
    * testing identifiers are not reserved words in C++/Stan
    * trapping/reporting locations of errors in data and init reads
    * improvements in dump data format reader for more R compatibility
      and more generality
    * fix bug in bernoulli logit distro tail density
-- Code Improvements
    * templated out matrix libs to reduce code duplication
    * vectorized auto-dif for tcrossprod() and crossprod()
    * optimizations in Wishart
    * vectorization with efficiency improvements in probability distributions
-- Libraries Updated
    * Eigen version 3.1.1 replaced with version 3.1.2
    * Boost version 1.51.0 replaced with version 1.52.0
-- Manual Improvements
    * New chapter on univariate and multivariate variable transforms
    * Many consistency improvements and typo corrections
    * Information on running command line in parallel from shell

====================================================================

Enjoy, and let us know if you run into any problems.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
On Wednesday, December 26, 2012 12:26:06 PM UTC-5, Jianling wrote:
> Hi,
>
> I am fitting a negative binomial glm as the following:
>
> Y_{k,i} ~ NB(phi, phi / mu_k )
>
> log(mu_k) = X_k \beta
>
> As you see, my data is clustered and I am not modeling any random
> effects, yet. This works well.
>
> But when I include an offset to mu_k:
>
> log(mu_k) = offset_k + X_k \beta
>
> Stan works a lot slower compared to the one without offset. I am not
> familiar with HMC so I'd appreciated if any one could point out the
> reason. And, is there any ways to speed up ?

I am surprised that simply including an offset would make a noticeable difference in the speed the evaluate the log-posterior. I would guess that it is increasing the rejection rate of proposals, perhaps due to overflow. In general, with GLM's it is often good to write some custom code for a few reasons. First, you can use whatever parameterization of the distribution you want, rather than the one(s) that come with Stan. Second, you can avoid some round-tripping of transformations that may introduce overflow or underflow. We've done so already with variants of the bernoulli and Poisson distributions, but not yet for the negative binomial, beta, etc.

It sounds like you might prefer the parameterization of the negative binomial in terms of the mean and dispersion, rather than the parameterization in Stan which utilizes a shape and an inverse scale parameter. If so, let me know and I'll work through the math / Stan code.

One simple thing that can be done is to vectorize the prior, rather than looping, i.e. do

beta ~ normal(0,1);

Ben

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Re: Speeding up the Cauchy function
messages.body_plain:
> On Wednesday, December 26, 2012 3:51:16 PM UTC-5, Ilya Esteban wrote:
>

>     ...  I am trying to refactor my code to express the Cauchy distribution as a ratio of two Normal
>     distributions....

>
>     Are there any better ways of speeding up sampling from the Cauchy? Thanks in advance!

The other problem with the ratio is that it's not identified.
Instead, I'd recommend relying directly on the inverse CDF as
Matt's been recommending, which is quite simple for the Cauchy,
assuming the Wikipedia page is right:

     http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cauchy_distribution#Related_distributions

If

     u ~ uniform(-pi/2, pi/2), and

     v = a + b * tan(y),

then

     v ~ cauchy(a,b);

To express in Stan, you'd declare:

   parameters {
     real<lower = -pi()/2, upper = pi()/2> u;
   }
   transformed parameters {
     real v;
     v <- a + b * tan(u);
   }

where a and b are declared as type real in
the data, transformed data, parameters, or transformed
parameters block.  Of course, you don't need a if it's
a constant 0 or b if it's a constant 1.

probably won't be any faster than just transforming
in a loop.  Also, the transformed parameter's just there
for convenience to print it.  You can either make it
a local variable (slightly faster as there's no printing
or range checking) or you can just use the expression
(a + b * tan(u)) where you would've used v and skip the
intermediate altogether.

On 12/26/12 3:35 PM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> On Wednesday, December 26, 2012 12:26:06 PM UTC-5, Jianling wrote:
>
>     Hi,
>
>     I am fitting a negative binomial glm as the following:
>
>     Y_{k,i} ~ NB(phi, phi / mu_k )
>
>     log(mu_k) = X_k \beta

This requires:

   mu_k <- exp(X_k * beta);

   inv_scale <- phi / mu_k;

This may be more arithmetically stable if you
implement it as:

   inv_scale <- exp(log(phi) - mu_k);

>     As you see, my data is clustered and I am not modeling any random
>     effects, yet. This works well.
>
>     But when I include an offset to mu_k:
>
>     log(mu_k) = offset_k + X_k \beta
>
>     Stan works a lot slower compared to the one without offset. I am not
>     familiar with HMC so I'd appreciated if any one could point out the
>     reason. And, is there any ways to speed up ?

The speed and stability for negative binomial will improve in our
next release.  We need to vectorize the gradient calcs and make
some of our own internal calcs more stable.  Right now, we evaluate

   log ( inv_scale / (1 - inv_scale) )

which would most likely be problematic in cases where inv_scale
is close to 0 or close to 1.  This should also be evaluated as:

   log(inv_scale) - log1m(inv_scale),

which should be much more arithmetically stable for inv_scale near
1 and somewhat more stable for inv_scale near 0.

We're also working on adding alternative parameterizations.

Vectorizing the negative binomial won't make things much faster
at the moment because the gradients aren't vectorized internally.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
On 12/26/12 5:00 PM, Jianling Zhong wrote:
> Thanks, Ben.
>
> When you say writing some custom code, do you mean code just for calculating the pmf or do you mean stan itself isn't
> suitable for this task yet? I wrote some mcmc R code before and the mixing isn't working well, that's why I tried stan
> and it seems working great, except for the slow speed in some cases.

> Maybe I can try to write the beta and negative binomial pmf myself in the stan model definition and see how it works.

You can always unfold directly and increment lp__ with
the log probabilities.

As we optimize more and more of the probability functions (we
first vectorized them so the language wouldn't change so much,
but we're going through and unfolding the gradient calcs and
doing algebra to reduce repeated computations with vectorization),
you shouldn't need to do this.

> As for the parameterization for the pmf, any form is fine, unless transforming the parameters takes a lot time ( which I
> assume doesn't ). I do have a suggesting, though:  the pmf's in stan can take vectors as parameters, but it internally

> sums up the log densities.Wouldn't it be easier to work with if it returns a vector, instead of returning a summation.

The reason it returns a single value is that we need to return a single
log probabilty in the end.  By taking the entire summation as a single
value, we can make the auto-dif more efficient.

Also, it doesn't compute them independently.  It will share
computations that only need to be done once.  That is, the
individual log densities often aren't even computed directly.
See the example of log(sigma) below.

> Another related, is it possible to add a 'count' parameter to the pmf functions? Then instead of calculating the log pmf
> for the same value multiple times,  it can just be calculated once and then multiplied by the 'count'.

We don't have any plans to add count features like this (other
than the obvious binomial and multinomial counting up bernoulli
and categorical pmfs).

The probability functions we've optimized already do this internally
for parameters if there are scalar parameters mixed with vector parameters.
So if you have

   y ~ normal(mu,sigma);

and y is a vector and sigma is a scalar, Stan will only
compute log(sigma) once.

But if you really just want to count the same data point y with the
same parameters mu and sigma a a total of N times, you can do, for instance

   for (n in 1:N)
      y ~ normal(mu,sigma);

but it's more efficient to just do as you suggest
and multiply because we're on the log scale:

   lp__ <- lp__ + N * normal_log(y,mu,sigma);

- Bob

There isn't a vectorized inv_logit, but we're working
on vectorizing all of the univariate scalar functions
to give them signatures:

    (real):real

    (real[]):real[]

    (vector):vector

    (row_vector):row_vector

    (matrix):matrix

Then we might also want to have all the vectors of these
things, such as for an array of vectors:

    (vector[]):vector[]

Right now, our priorities are speeding up all the probability function and
matrix op gradient calculations (the main speed bottleneck), vectorizing the
multivariate probability functions, and adding cumulative distribution functions
(which require a bunch of new special functions for gradients).

So vectorizing the basic functions is probably still a few months out.

- Bob

>
>

Phi_norm ~ normal(0,1);

Thanks very much for the diagnositics.  As Daniel suggests, I need to switch to running stan from the command line to capture runtime errors (to eliminate the possibility of crashing R).   Anyway, now everything is working.  Some comments related to your comments:

1. putting anything to the left of a ~ where scalars are passed to the distribution works when a is an array of scalar elements.  It will not compile, for example, for "z" under the following declaration:  vector[beta] z[K];  - presumably because each element of z is a vector.  Anyway, your tip (as always) is very helpful.  Will the user find it in the documentation?

3. I will report back the run properties of this model.  It is a magilla/ginormous multivariate model and, if it samples efficiently, that's really exciting for  the possibilities of using stan under multiple response types.

terrance.

messages.body_plain:
It looks a doable model in Stan.  One issue, which can be solved here, is that Stan does not support discrete sampling yet, so the following is problematic,

ind2[d] ~ bernoulli(0.5) ;

But you can easily integrate out ind2 here and use a mixture for beta2.  Since you care more about ind2, you can get back to it when you have beta2.

--
Jiqiang

On Sun, Dec 30, 2012 at 5:37 AM, Marcel Jonker <mfjo...@hotmail.com> wrote:

> Dear STAN users,
>
> I am trying to estimate a panel-data model with AR2 errors:
>
> for (i in 1:N){  #20 regions
>  for (t in 1:T){  #35 years
>   M[i,t] <- alpha[i] + inprod(beta1[]*X1[i,t,]) + inprod(beta2[],X2[i,t,])
>   Err[i,t] <- Y[i,t] - M[i,t]
>  }
>  for (t in 3:T){
>   Y[i,t] ~ normal( mu[i,t] , tau )
>   mu[i,t] <- M[i,t] + rho[1]*Err[i,t-1] + rho[2]*Err[i,t-2]
> }}

> This model is still a basic copy of the previous OpenBUGS implementation, which means that I have not yet looked at the best way to vectorize the code. Anyway, X1 contains a (relatively small) set of explanatory variables that are always included in the model specification, whereas X2 contains a large set of dummies of which only one or two are likely to be included. Hence the following prior is placed on beta2[]:
>
> for (d in 1:30){
>  ind2[d] ~ bernoulli(0.5) ;
>  beta2[d] ~ normal( 0 , ind2[d]*100 + (1-ind2[d]) * 0.3 );
> }

> The values of mean=0 and stdev=0.3 are based on a prior runs of the model without variable selection, and allows for the sampling from a more informative prior when ind2 is 0. Also, for reporting purposes, the inference on ind2 (i.e. whether or not the X2 variables are included in the model specification) is more important than the estimated value of beta2[]. Is it possible to estimate this model using STAN - e.g. using the method described in chapter 9 of the manual? And perhaps someone has a suggestion on how to actually do this, if possible? Thank you!
>
> Best regards,
> Marcel Jonker

messages.subject: lgamma numeric overflow and debug?
messages.subject_clean: lgamma numeric overflow and debug?
messages.body_plain:
Hi, there,

I think this really is not a lgamma problem. The problem may be in my model or how the parameter values are initialized. I'd appreciate if anyone could help me to debug it.

The stan file is attached. Here is what I am trying to do:

I am modeling some count data with excessive number of zeros. I tried zero inflated poisson and zero inflated negative binomial. The later worked reasonably well but it sometimes overly inflated the zero part. So I decided to try some random effects / mixture model. My data amount is huge ( total data points on the order of 10^7, it's genomic sequencing data ), so I need a mixture model that the marginal distribution of the count has a close form.

I am trying to put a beta mixing distribution on the failure probability of the negative binomial ( not sure if it's the right thing to do). And the marginal distribution of the count is the following form:

\frac{ gamma(phi + y) }{gamma(phi) * gamma(y + 1)}  * \frac{gamma(phi + alpha) * gamma(alpha + beta)}{ gamma(phi + alpha + beta) * gamma(alpha) }

y is the count response, phi, alpha and beta are the parameters for the negative binomial and the mixing beta distribution. In the stan file, I unfold the beta function to gamma function, and separated the zero counts with nonzero counts. And also did some other things to save some computation.

Here is the problem:

When I ran the model, sometimes there is no problem except an warning message:

" Informational Message: The parameter state is about to be Metropolis rejected due to the following underlying, non-fatal (really) issue (and please ignore that what comes next might say 'error'): Error in function boost::math::lgamma<e>(e): Evaluation of lgamma at a negative integer 0.
If the problem persists across multiple draws, you might have a problem with an initial state or a gradient somewhere.
 If the problem does not persist, the resulting samples will still be drawn from the posterior. "

But most of the time I got a numeric overflow error for lgamma:

Exception: Error in function boost::math::lgamma<d>(d): numeric overflow
Diagnostic information:
Throw location unknown (consider using BOOST_THROW_EXCEPTION)
Dynamic exception type: boost::exception_detail::clone_impl<boost::exception_detail::error_info_injector<std::overflow_error> >
std::exception::what: Error in function boost::math::lgamma<d>(d): numeric overflow

Since the model runs sometimes, so I think the problem is in my model. But I don't know how to debug it and am not sure the model is appropriate. Thanks for any help to identify the problem.

Also, an related question: how do I debug the code besides using print statement? The error message says using BOOST_THROW_EXCEPTION. How can I use it and compile the binary so the error message would be more informative?

Thanks a lot!

Jianling
